code.title: Pure vs impure functions and injected time

followUps:
Not in the strict sense, because throwing is an observable effect besides returning a value. In practice many teams still treat it as pure: for the same input it always throws the same error and changes nothing outside.

The cleaner option is to return a value that represents failure, for example { ok: false, error: 'negative' }, so callers handle it as ordinary data. Either way the function stays deterministic and easy to test: parse('-1') always gives the same result.

Yes, mutating variables that only exist inside the function is fine, because nobody outside can observe it. Purity is judged by inputs and outputs, not by how the body is written.

Example: let s = 0; for (const x of xs) s += x; mutates s but is pure, and is often faster than chaining reduce. The line is crossed when you mutate an argument or shared object: xs.sort() changes the caller's array, while [...xs].sort() does not.

Pass the time in as a parameter or inject a clock instead of calling Date.now() inside the logic. Then a test chooses the time.

const isExpired = (t, now) => now >= t.expiresAt;
isExpired({ expiresAt: 1000 }, 999);  // false
isExpired({ expiresAt: 1000 }, 1000); // true

At the edge you call isExpired(t, Date.now()). Alternatively use fake timers such as jest.useFakeTimers().setSystemTime(...).

code.title: Shallow copy, deep copy and structural sharing

followUps:
It gives wrong or failing results whenever the value holds something JSON cannot represent. Dates become strings, undefined and functions are dropped, NaN and Infinity become null, and Map, Set and RegExp become {} or lose their contents.

Circular references throw a TypeError, and BigInt throws too. Example: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ d: new Date(0), u: undefined })) returns { d: '1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' }. structuredClone handles dates, maps, sets and cycles, but still not functions.

Immer hands your code a draft, a proxy wrapping the current state, and records every write you make to it. When your function finishes, it builds the result by copying only the nodes that were written to, plus their ancestors, and reusing every other node unchanged.

const next = produce(state, d => { d.items.a.push(3); });
next.items.b === state.items.b; // true, untouched
next !== state;                 // true, new root

If nothing is written, it returns the same reference. Cost is proportional to the changed path, plus proxy overhead.

code.title: pipe and compose

followUps:
Make the first function special: let it accept any number of arguments and return one value, then feed the rest of the pipeline normally. Only the first step needs this, because every later step receives exactly one value.

const pipe = (first, ...rest) =>
  (...args) => rest.reduce((acc, f) => f(acc), first(...args));
pipe(Math.max, x => x * 2)(3, 9, 4); // 18

Here Math.max takes three numbers and the next step doubles the result.

Insert a tap step that logs the value and returns it unchanged, then move it along the pipeline to see where the data goes wrong.

const tap = label => x => (console.log(label, x), x);
pipe(trim, tap('after trim'), upper, tap('after upper'))(' hi ');

Also name each step instead of using inline arrows so stack traces show useful names, and test each small function alone. Splitting a long pipeline into named sub-pipelines works because composition is associative.

Each Koa or Express middleware is a function that does some work and hands control to the next one, so the chain is a composition of functions. Koa's compose runs mw[i](ctx, () => dispatch(i + 1)), which is the same idea as pipe, except each step also gets a next function and can run code before and after it.

Example: a logger calls await next() and then prints the elapsed time. That wrapping behaviour makes it an onion model rather than a plain one-way pipe.

code.title: Currying vs partial application

followUps:
Add a placeholder value, such as a unique symbol, that marks an argument slot to be filled in later. Each call fills the placeholder slots from left to right first, then appends any extra arguments.

const _ = Symbol('ph');
function merge(saved, more) {
  const out = saved.map(a => a === _ && more.length ? more.shift() : a);
  return out.concat(more);
}
// ready when out.length >= fn.length and has no _

Example: c(_, 2)(1)(3) on a three-argument function gives f(1, 2, 3).

Return a function that remembers a running total and, when called with no arguments, returns it. Otherwise it adds the argument and returns itself.

function sum(a) {
  let total = a;
  const next = b => b === undefined ? total : (total += b, next);
  return next;
}
sum(1)(2)(3)(); // 6

The empty call is the stop signal, since JavaScript cannot know how many calls are coming. Another trick is overriding valueOf so +sum(1)(2)(3) works.

It hurts when the arity is unclear, the argument order does not match how people want to partially apply it, or the code is on a hot path. Each partial call allocates a new closure and an args array, so in a loop of a million items it is measurably slower than a plain call.

Debugging is harder too, since stack traces show anonymous wrappers. Also fn.length ignores defaults and rest parameters, so a curried function with an optional argument can fire too early. Use currying for configuration-style functions, such as fetchWith(baseUrl)(path), and plain calls elsewhere.

code.title: Memoize with LRU bound and promise caching

followUps:
Because the default key is just the first argument, which is fast and enough for one-argument functions, and the cache key must be a single value. The key is then used directly in a Map, so memoize(f)(1, 2) and memoize(f)(1, 3) collide and the second call wrongly returns the first result.

Lodash lets you pass a resolver, for example memoize(f, (a, b) => a + ':' + b), to build a key from all arguments. The design avoids guessing how to hash objects, which would be slow or wrong. The cache is also exposed as .cache.

Store the in-flight promise in the cache straight away, so every concurrent caller for the same key receives the same promise and only one real request is made. If 100 requests ask for key u1 while the first is pending, the backend sees 1 call, not 100.

if (!cache.has(k))
  cache.set(k, fn(k).catch(e => { cache.delete(k); throw e; }));
return cache.get(k);

Remove it on failure so errors are not cached. Add a TTL to avoid stale data, and jitter expiry times so many keys do not expire together.

code.title: Debounce and throttle on a fake clock

followUps:
Debounce waits for quiet and runs once at the end, so a steady stream of calls could postpone it forever. maxWait sets an upper limit on that delay and forces a call after that many ms even if calls keep arriving.

Example: debounce(save, 1000, { maxWait: 5000 }) with a user typing nonstop for 20 seconds would otherwise never save. With maxWait it saves at roughly 5, 10, 15 and 20 seconds. Throttle in lodash is implemented as exactly this combination.

Create the debounced function once and keep it stable across renders, because a new one on every render has its own timer and the debouncing is lost. Use useMemo or useRef, or wrap it in useCallback, and cancel it in the effect cleanup.

const send = useMemo(() => debounce(q => search(q), 300), []);
useEffect(() => () => send.cancel(), [send]);

Alternatively debounce the value: keep a debounced state updated by a timer in an effect, and fetch when that value changes.

Replace real time with a fake clock: jest or vitest fake timers, or a clock object you pass in. The test then advances time by exact amounts and finishes instantly.

vi.useFakeTimers();
const f = debounce(spy, 100);
f(); vi.advanceTimersByTime(99);  // spy not called
vi.advanceTimersByTime(1);        // spy called once

Check calls at 99 ms and 100 ms, bursts, cancel and flush. The test takes microseconds, not 100 ms, and never flakes.

code.title: Testing debounce with fake timers

followUps:
Because real sleeps depend on the machine's scheduler, so the same test passes on your laptop and fails on a busy CI server. A timer set for 100 ms may fire at 101, 130 or 300 ms, and a test that sleeps 110 ms and expects one call can see zero.

The usual fixes of longer sleeps make the suite slow: 200 tests sleeping 0.5 s cost 100 seconds. Fake timers remove both problems, since time only moves when the test says so and ordering is exact.

Fake timers control setTimeout and Date.now, but promise callbacks run in the microtask queue, which is not advanced by them. So advanceTimersByTime may run your timer, yet the .then that follows has not run when the next line executes.

Use the async variants, such as await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(100) or await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(100), which flush microtasks between timers. Otherwise add await Promise.resolve() after advancing. Some setups also fake queueMicrotask, so check the configuration.

code.title: Layout thrashing modelled with a counter

followUps:
Properties handled by the compositor on the GPU, without layout or paint, are transform and opacity, plus filter in many browsers. Changing them can run smoothly even when the main thread is busy.

Animating left, top, width or height triggers layout, and background-color triggers paint. So move an element with transform: translateX(100px) instead of left: 100px. The hint will-change: transform can promote a layer, but overuse costs GPU memory.

INP (Interaction to Next Paint) measures how long the page takes to visually respond after a click, tap or key press, using roughly the worst interaction in the visit. It replaced FID as a Core Web Vital.

Good is 200 ms or less, 200 to 500 ms needs improvement, and above 500 ms is poor, measured at the 75th percentile of real users. Layout thrashing and long tasks in event handlers are common causes. Break up long work with scheduler.yield() or setTimeout, so the browser can paint.

React batches state updates and commits them to the DOM together, and useLayoutEffect runs right after the DOM is updated but before the browser paints, so reading geometry there is correct and sees final layout. The danger is that reading forces layout, and if your effect then sets state, React re-renders synchronously and you can pay for layout twice.

Keep reads in one effect, avoid read-write-read cycles across several layout effects, and use useEffect when you do not need to block painting. Measuring 100 items in one effect costs one layout; measuring each in its own effect can cost 100.

code.title: EventEmitter with once, off and snapshot emit

followUps:
Wildcards need matching by pattern instead of an exact key lookup. Keep exact listeners in the Map, and keep pattern listeners in a second list, then on each emit run both.

emit(ev, ...a) {
  exact(ev).forEach(f => f(...a));
  for (const [pat, f] of this.patterns)
    if (match(pat, ev)) f(ev, ...a);
}

For user.*, split names on dots and compare parts, or compile the pattern to a regex once at subscribe time. A trie keyed by name segments is faster with thousands of patterns.

Always remove listeners when the component is destroyed, because the emitter holds a reference to each callback and keeps its whole closure alive, even after the component is gone. In React return the unsubscribe from the effect: useEffect(() => emitter.on('x', h), []), since on returns the cleanup function.

Other safeguards are an AbortSignal passed to the listener registration, a max-listener warning (Node warns at 10), and counting listeners in tests. A page navigated 100 times that adds 3 listeners each time and never removes them leaks 300.

code.title: Singleton with a cached promise

followUps:
Give the singleton an explicit reset function, or better, avoid the global and inject the instance. For module singletons, tests can call jest.resetModules() and re-import, so the module is evaluated again and creates a new instance.

beforeEach(() => { jest.resetModules(); });
const { db } = require('./db'); // fresh instance

Or export resetForTests() that clears the cached instance. Needing this at all is a sign that dependency injection would be simpler.

Because a module is loaded once per server process and then shared by every request, so anything stored in a module-level variable is visible to all users. If request 1 stores user A's profile in a global let current and request 2 reads it, user B can see A's data, especially with async code interleaving.

Key the cache by user or tenant id, store per-request data in the request context (or AsyncLocalStorage), and bound the cache size. Serverless adds a surprise: the same instance may serve many requests, or be created per container.

code.title: Factory functions vs classes

followUps:
Because the factory is the place where dependencies are chosen, tests can hand it fakes. A function like makeUserService({ db, clock }) gets a fake db and a fixed clock in the test, with no mocking library and no patching of globals.

const svc = makeUserService({ db: fakeDb, clock: () => 1000 });
svc.isExpired(user); // uses the fake clock

Each test makes a new instance, so no state is shared between tests.

An abstract factory is an object that creates a whole family of related objects, for example a darkTheme factory that makes dark buttons and dark inputs, while lightTheme makes the light versions. The caller uses one interface and never names concrete classes.

In JavaScript you rarely need the formal pattern: an object of functions, such as { button: () => ..., input: () => ... }, does the job, because functions are first-class and there are no interfaces to declare. Pass the chosen object in as a parameter.

code.title: Search box race: stale response vs abort

followUps:
Yes, both are needed because they solve different problems. Debounce reduces how many requests are sent: typing 'react' sends one request instead of five. AbortController (or an id check) fixes correctness: a response for 're' that arrives after the one for 'react' must not be shown.

Debounce alone still allows races, since a slow request can still return late, and abort alone still floods the server. Together they save bandwidth and prevent stale results. Servers also benefit when aborts cancel work.

Keep the highlighted index in one piece of state (or in a ref and the DOM), and update only the two rows that change, rather than rebuilding the list. Memoize the row component with React.memo so only the old and the new active row re-render.

Use the aria-activedescendant pattern: focus stays in the input, ArrowUp and ArrowDown change the active id, and the list only toggles a class or aria-selected. With a virtualized list of 10,000 results, only about 15 rows exist in the DOM, so a key press touches 2 of them.

code.title: Functional core, imperative shell

followUps:
Allow it where nobody else can see it or where measurement shows a need: local variables inside a function, a freshly created array you are still building, a performance-critical loop, or a cache and counters that are private to a module.

Example: building a 1,000,000-element result with push in a loop is fine, while spreading [...acc, x] inside reduce copies the array each time and costs O(n squared). Keep the mutation hidden behind a function whose inputs and outputs stay immutable.

Start small and show benefits, rather than announcing a rewrite. Pick one painful area, such as a bug-prone reducer or a date utility, rewrite it as pure functions with tests, and share the result.

Then add lightweight guardrails: lint rules against mutation (no-param-reassign), a shared utility file with a few named helpers, and code review habits that ask 'can this be pure?'. Run short pairing sessions, avoid heavy point-free style at first, and agree that readability wins over cleverness. Revisit after a month using bug and test metrics.

Type checking catches structural mistakes, but not behavioural ones. Types catch wrong argument types, a missing null check, wrong return shape, and misuse of readonly (so some accidental mutation).

Tests are needed for the timing and state bugs: this forwarding, caching a rejection, an unbounded cache, a debounced function recreated on each render, iteration over a live array during emit, and layout read/write interleaving. Those are all about runtime order and values, which types do not describe. Use both: types for shape, tests with fake timers for behaviour.

Give the agent a measurable goal and a loop: record a baseline profile, change one thing, record again, and keep the change only if the number improves. Name the metric (INP, long tasks, number of forced layouts) and the page action to test.

A prompt could say: 'Profile the search page with a Performance trace while typing 10 characters, list tasks over 50 ms, fix the biggest one, re-measure, and show before and after numbers.' Require it to explain each fix, run the tests, and not remove features. Review the diff yourself.
